reason: The chapter says radioactive decay heats young bodies, so applying it to rocky planetesimals is a plausible start toward separating their interiors.
expectation: The rocky bodies should heat internally, potentially allowing rock and metal to separate.

alternatives.reason: Heating icy bodies may also advance the goal of altering water-bearing rock.

effect: The rocky planetesimal has melted, making internal separation plausible.
reaction: The qualification that not all asteroids melt is useful.
reason: Gravity can pull dense metal inward in a melted body, separating it from rocky material.
expectation: The molten body should differentiate into a metal-rich interior and rocky outer layers.

effect: Gravity separated metal from silicate; the outer rock must cool before collisions can expose fragments.
reaction: The cooling prerequisite makes the sequence clear.
reason: Escaping radiation should cool and solidify the layered body before it breaks apart.
expectation: The planetesimal’s outer rocky layers should solidify.

effect: The asteroid’s rocky exterior has solidified, so collisions can now break it apart.
reaction: The cooling step makes the sequence physically clear.
reason: Collisions should break the differentiated asteroid and expose its rocky and metal-rich layers.
expectation: The collision should produce fragments of rock and metal from the asteroid.

effect: The collision exposed rocky-layer fragments and completed the stone-and-metal goal; the water-bearing rock goal remains.
reaction: The result mentions other fragments, but the goal completion confirms the intended outcome.
reason: Radioactive heating may melt ice inside an icy planetesimal, allowing water to react with rock.
expectation: The icy body should warm enough for liquid water to become available inside it.

effect: Internal heating produced confined liquid water, making a reaction with rock possible.
reaction: The contrast between a frozen exterior and liquid water inside is interesting.
reason: Silicate grains are the available rocky material that could react with the liquid water.

choice.combine: Liquid water inside an icy body

expectation: Water should alter the silicate rock and become incorporated into water-bearing minerals.

effect: Water reacted with silicates to form hydrated asteroid rock, completing the remaining goal and showing how hydrogen can be carried in minerals.
reaction: The possibility of water-bearing rock surviving after exposed ice is gone was interesting.

mostWorthwhile.text: Making hydrated rock was most worthwhile: the heating and reaction showed how a frozen-looking body can develop liquid water and incorporate it into minerals.

leastWorthwhile.text: The collision result was somewhat confusing: it named rocky-layer fragments and referred to other fragments, yet completed the stone-and-metal goal without explicitly showing metal fragments.

surprise.text: I was surprised that a frozen exterior can conceal liquid water and water–rock reactions inside.

arbitrary.text: No action felt especially arbitrary; the cooling and collision sequence had a clear physical purpose.

continue.text: Yes. I would continue to see how hydrated asteroid material contributes to Earth's formation; the chapter connected straightforward combinations to useful physical processes.
